entities.summary:
Jan Tarnowski (died 1605) served as the influential Archbishop of Gniezno and Primate of Poland from 1603 until his death, a pivotal ecclesiastical role during the tumultuous early decades of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth's Golden Liberty era. As Primate, he was the senior-most cleric, wielding not only spiritual authority over the Catholic Church in Poland but also significant political power, notably acting as Interrex during periods of royal interregnum. His tenure coincided with the reign of Sigismund III Vasa, a period marked by intense religious debate, the strengthening of the Counter-Reformation, and the ongoing struggle between the monarch and the powerful magnate families of the szlachta.

Elevated to the primacy following a distinguished career, Tarnowski was previously Bishop of Poznań (1600–1603) and Bishop of Kujawy (1595–1600). His ecclesiastical career saw him navigate the complex religious landscape of the Commonwealth, where Catholicism, Protestantism, and Eastern Orthodoxy coexisted, albeit with increasing pressure from the Counter-Reformation. As Primate, he presided over the Polish Senate, held the right to crown kings, and, crucially, assumed the powers of the monarch between reigns, summoning the convocation and election sejms (parliaments) to choose a new king. His Rola coat of arms symbolized his noble lineage, a common prerequisite for high office in the Commonwealth.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Jan Tarnowski, as Primate of Poland and Archbishop of Gniezno, held one of the most powerful positions in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, embodying both spiritual and temporal authority. His role as Interrex maintained constitutional order during royal transitions, a unique feature that prevented civil strife in an elective monarchy.
